newsitem.title: GERMANY: Military count Zaire refugees, examine scenarios.
newsitem.headline: Military count Zaire refugees, examine scenarios.

text.p: Western and African military leaders met on Friday to discuss sending troops to ease Zaire's refugee crisis, but failed even to agree on the number of refugees and said their talks would go on into the weekend.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission, told a news conference that estimates presented at the meeting of the number of refugees in need of help varied between 100,000 and 500,000.
"We're going to find out (how many there are) before we commit any troops," he told a news conference near the meeting at U.S. European Command headquarters in Stuttgart, Germany.
"By the end of the weekend I would hope we will have developed a full slate of options."

Three scenarios laid out in a preliminary discussion document seen by Reuters set out the pros and cons of basing a military relief operation in Rwanda or in Zaire and included a third option of not sending any extra troops at all.

Baril said the initial focus of the talks was on narrowing down estimates of the number of refugees. "A firm commitment (to send troops) can only be made later by governments after they have considered all the options," he added.
He refused to be drawn on how many troops, if any, such a mission might require, but said there appeared to be between 100,000 and 250,000 refugees requiring help.
But he added: "The mandate we have is to open a (relief) corridor to those who really need it...We're not here to feed and transport them, but to open the corridor."

A major problem for nations wanting to help has been the fluidity of the situation in eastern Zaire, where hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees have been displaced by a conflict pitting Rwandan-backed Zairean Tutsi rebels against Zairean government forces and Rwandan Hutu militias.
U.S. Brigadier General John Casey said one problem was finding out how many displaced people were Rwandan refugees and not Zaireans displaced within their own country.
A military official at the talks confirmed that the paper seen by Reuters set out scenarios which provided the basis for early discussions by the military planners.
It noted many nations were geared up to provide relief from Rwanda, and this option would probably only need light security.
But it would require approval from Rwanda, which has so far been reluctant to see a multinational operation on its soil.
Providing relief from a base in Zaire however would mean establishing a secure headquarters, probably with heavy forces.
The paper said the idea had support from Kinshasa, but carried a bigger risk of getting embroiled in conflict.

It would also limit efforts to repatriate to Rwanda the Hutu refugees who fled from Tutsi forces after the 1994 Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis. It would need more complex logistical suppport than a Rwanda-based operation, and take more time.
In a third option, external forces would maintain low-level operational help they now give to Rwanda and relief agencies.
The official, who asked not to be named, said all the scenarios would be likely to undergo extensive revision.
Britain, France and Spain say a force is still needed despite the recent return of half a million refugees to Rwanda.
But Washington has cancelled plans to send combat troops and has instead begun preparing for an airlift in which the U.S. military would provide logistics.

Several African nations -- including Zimbabwe, Botswana, Cameroon, Senegal and South Africa -- were present at the talks as well as representatives from the major Western powers. But there were no representatives from either Zaire or Rwanda.
